summary: An experimental proposal for a Content-Disposition header that lets MIME messages convey presentation information, such as whether a part should be shown inline or treated as an attachment. It was replaced by RFC 2183.

eli5.summary: A sticky note on part of an email saying whether to show it right away or save it separately.

questions: how do email attachments know to be attachments
subtitle: A header that tells email clients whether to show message parts inline or as downloadable attachments.

tldr.problem: MIME messages can contain multiple parts, but senders have no standard way to tell receivers whether each part should be displayed immediately (inline) or saved separately (attachment). Mail clients have to guess, leading to inconsistent behavior.
tldr.mechanism: The Content-Disposition header uses two values: "inline" for parts to display immediately, and "attachment" for parts to save separately. An optional filename parameter suggests a name if the recipient saves the part to a file.
tldr.outcome: Mail clients can now respect the sender's intent about how to present message parts, and attachments can be stored with a suggested filename, improving user experience across different email systems.

today: This RFC is Experimental. RFC 2183 supersedes it and refines the specification. The Content-Disposition header is now a standard part of email systems worldwide.

sections.title: The Problem: How Should Email Parts Be Displayed?
sections.content:
MIME introduced the ability to send multiple types of content in a single email message—text, images, audio and more. However, MIME did not specify how mail clients should present these parts to users. A client might receive a message with an image, a text note, and a spreadsheet, but the RFC did not say whether the image should appear inline in the message body or presented as a separate attachment. Different mail clients made different choices, leading to a confusing user experience.

This RFC proposes a simple mechanism to let the sender indicate the desired presentation. Some parts should be displayed automatically when the message is viewed (inline), while others should be shown as separate attachments that the user opens intentionally. The mechanism also allows senders to suggest a filename for saving attachments.
sections.eli5: Email messages can have pictures, files and other stuff in them, but the program reading the email didn't know whether to show them right away or wait for you to click to see them. This header tells it what to do.

sections.title: The Content-Disposition Header
sections.content:
The Content-Disposition header is optional and can be placed on any MIME message part. Its syntax is simple: it specifies a disposition type ("inline" or "attachment", or a future extension), followed by optional parameters. The header is case-insensitive. An example inline part might be Content-Disposition: inline, while an attachment might be Content-Disposition: attachment; filename=genome.jpeg.

The specification explicitly allows for future extension. Unrecognized disposition types should be treated as "attachment" as a safe default (the assumption is that if a sender goes to the trouble of specifying a new disposition type, they intend something more elaborate than inline display). Unrecognized parameters should be ignored. Parameters apply to all disposition types unless otherwise specified, so the filename parameter works with both inline and attachment dispositions.
sections.eli5: The header is a simple label: "inline" means show it now, "attachment" means save it. You can add a filename parameter to suggest what to call the file if someone saves it.

sections.title: Inline and Attachment Disposition Types
sections.content:
An inline disposition means the mail client should display the body part automatically when the message is viewed, in the order it appears among other parts. Inline parts are presented as part of the message body. An attachment disposition means the part should not be displayed automatically; instead, the user must take explicit action (clicking a link, running a command) to view it. Mail clients might show attachments as a list or with icons, leaving it to the user to decide whether to open them.

The specification also clarifies how dispositions apply to multipart messages. If a multipart body part is marked as "attachment", the entire multipart is withheld until the user chooses to view it; the dispositions of the subparts are then consulted when the multipart is displayed. If a multipart is marked as "inline", it displays normally, but the dispositions of subparts are still respected (so an inline part within the multipart displays immediately, but an attachment subpart requires action).
sections.eli5: "Inline" means the email program shows it right away when you open the message. "Attachment" means the program shows you a list of files you can click to open. For multipart messages, if the whole thing is an attachment, you have to open that first before seeing the parts inside.

sections.title: The Filename Parameter and Security
sections.content:
The filename parameter suggests a name for the body part if the recipient saves it to a file. For example, Content-Disposition: attachment; filename=report.pdf suggests that the part be saved as "report.pdf". However, the RFC emphasizes that the receiving mail client must not blindly use the sender's suggested filename. The client should check that the filename conforms to local filesystem conventions, does not overwrite an existing file, and does not create security risks.

The RFC details specific security hazards. On UNIX systems, a filename like ".login" could create or modify a startup script, a path like "/etc/passwd" could overwrite a system file, or a filename like "../bin/trojan" could place an executable in a command search path. The client must ignore any directory path information in the filename and use only the terminal component (the filename part after any slashes). Additionally, the client should never name or place a file such that it will be automatically executed without explicit user action.
sections.eli5: The email can suggest a filename, but the email program must be careful not to let a trick filename overwrite important files or run commands automatically. It ignores any path information and only uses the basic filename.

sections.title: Examples of Content-Disposition Use
sections.content:
The RFC provides three examples. The first shows a JPEG image marked as inline with a description: Content-Type: image/jpeg followed by Content-Disposition: inline. The second shows the same image as an attachment with a suggested filename: Content-Disposition: attachment; filename=genome.jpeg. The third is a complete multipart message where the main text is inline, one multipart subpart is marked as attachment, and within that subpart, one piece is inline and another is attachment, illustrating the nesting rules.

These examples show how different dispositions work in practice and how multipart structures allow mixing inline and attachment parts in a single message.
sections.eli5: An example shows a picture marked to display right away. Another example shows the same picture marked as an attachment with a suggested filename. A third example shows a message with mixed inline and attachment parts to show how it all works together.

sections.title: Status and Evolution
sections.content: This RFC is marked Experimental. RFC 2183 refines and updates this specification, making it a draft standard. The basic concept of Content-Disposition has become fundamental to modern email: every email client today uses or recognizes this header (or its successor) to decide whether to show an attachment as a clickable item or as part of the message body. The header is now a de facto standard for message part presentation.
sections.eli5: This was an experimental RFC that helped prove the idea worked. Later, RFC 2183 refined it into a standard that email programs use today. Almost every email program now recognizes this header.
